articles.text: During the May 6 school board meeting, an empassioned discussion took place about a policy dictating the possession and use of mobile devices by students while at school. articles.text: Following the retirement last week of Planning Director Kevin Jackson, Piedmont City Council appointed Jeff Bond as the interim Planning Director. Bond will oversee the Planning Department’s ongoing projects until a permanent replacement is found. The city is working with Bob Murray & Associates to search for qualified candidates to fill the position. Bond is a professional with more than 30 years of experience. In July of 2025, he retired from the City of Albany, where he served for 20 years, the last 14 as Director of Community Development. He has a master’s degree in economics and is certified as a Chief Building Official, Residential Building Inspector, and American Institute Certified Planner. Before joining the City of Albany, Bond was a staff member at UC Berkeley involved in Interim Planning Director Jeff Bond campus planning, student housing development, and real estate initiatives. He also worked for the City of Alameda for several years as development manager, responsible for redevelopment projects, including the reuse of US Navy property. Early in his career, he worked for several land consulting firms, an economic development non-profit organization, and as a staff person in the California State Legislature. Bond has been with a variety of professional organizations, most recently as a board member of the APA California Northern Section and the Northern California Chapter of the Earthquake Engineering Research Institute. He was involved in curating the Urban Land Institute’s Urban Plan curriculum for high school students. “It is an honor to be considered for this appointment. You have a lovely community. I look forward to the chance to work with your wonderful staff and keep the momentum going,” said Bond at the council meeting on May 4. The application deadline for the position is May 24. articles.text: On Monday, May 4, Piedmont’s City Council approved a $142,236 contract for the Bonita Avenue parking and striping. It is anticipated that the work will begin in June after the last day of school. The contract documents allow for 20 working days to complete the work. The project should be completed before the first day of school on August 7. This project completes the remaining portion of the Civic Center restriping effort on Bonita Avenue from Oakland Avenue to Vista Avenue. The majority of restriping in the Civic Center area was completed as part of the 2025 Pavement Project. This segment was excluded at that time due to installation timing conflicts with the schedule for Havens Elementary School. The project includes converting Bonita Avenue to a one-way street with northbound vehicular traffic only, installing angled parking stalls along the easterly side of the roadway adjacent to Havens School, and adding two on-street angled accessible parking stalls. The city awarded the contract to D’s General Engineering of Oakland. The total budget for the project is $156,460, with funding coming from Measure BB (Local Streets and Roads), Vehicle Registration Fee (VRF), and California Senate Bill 1 (SB-1). Measure H provides around 20% of our school district’s annual budget, roughly $12 million. When we invest in our community schools, we invest in everyone’s road to success. According to the California Youth & Families Speak initiative – a statewide alliance of community organizing and advocacy groups advancing a shared vision of racially just, relationship-centered community schools – true community schools have seen student test scores improve by what would be the equivalent of having 151 more days of learning per school year. When we invest in our schools and allow them to become true community spaces—which requires adequate funding—students in Piedmont will continue to find elevated educational opportunities and facilities. By paying a parcel tax, we make our schools stronger and with that the property values also increase. Please vote yes on Measure H. –Andson Zhou Measure H will increase property taxes in Piedmont Editor: Supporters say the funding is needed to maintain services and schools. But voters should ask a basic question: How will they measure whether the additional money produces results? Measure H does not answer that. The measure outlines spending priorities but sets no benchmarks for success. Without benchmarks, the public cannot evaluate whether additional funding improves outcomes or simply increases spending. That matters because public funding moves through layers of administration, planning, and district decisions before residents see the effects. By then, the connection between spending and results becomes difficult to verify. Measure H also creates no standard for public review. There is no measure of success or failure and no way to compare promises with actual results. At the same time, additional property taxes add to already high housing and living costs in Piedmont. If voters approve ongoing taxes, they should also have a way to evaluate whether those taxes produce results. articles.text: This month Caltrans is presenting two in-person meetings at St. Jarlath’s Church in Oakland, on May 16 and May 23. These meetings will be the only opportunity for the public to voice their opinions on Caltrans’ study on lifting the ban on big-rig trucks on I-580. Seating is limited, and you need to register in advance to attend. The meetings start at 10 a.m. and doors open at 9:45 a.m. People may speak for up to five minutes. In the early 1960s, during the construction of I-580 (the MacArthur Freeway), the city of Oakland enacted City Ordinance No. 6789, which prohibits trucks weighing over 4.5 tons from using I-580 between Grand Avenue and San Leandro. The ban has effectively kept large trucks from entering Highway 13 (the Warren Freeway) as well as most neighborhood streets and connecting corridors. Now, after more than 60 years, Caltrans is considering whether to repeal this ban. In early 2025, Caltrans launched a truck access study to answer how removing the truck weight restriction on I-580 would affect safety, efficiency, reliability, and traffic speed, and how this change would impact public health equity for nearby communities. Caltrans is responding to community concerns and implementing strategies recommended by the West Oakland Community Action Plan (2019) to help improve community health. Judy Cain, a representative of the group NoBigRigs580, believes the truck ban helps protect communities from pollution and traffic risks, and removing it would harm the health and safety of neighborhoods. She believes the true reason large trucks are being considered for I-580 is for improved freight efficiency. According to NoBigRigs580, the California Trucking Association has a longstanding history of lobbying Caltrans to abandon the truck ban to improve freight efficiency. The beneficiary of a repeal would be the trucking companies’ business, rather than the health and safety of civilians. Opening I-580 to big-rig trucks will increase the number of trucks traveling through Oakland to and from the Port as the trucking industry maximizes the additional roadway capacity from I-580. Repealing the ban would knowingly increase the number of people exposed to truck pollution. The group is concerned about the increased noise pollution and safety risks that come with heavy A fully loaded big rig can weigh up to 80,000 pounds. trucks. The hills around the highway would make it difficult for sound walls to be effective. This would impact schools, hospitals, parks, and neighborhoods adjacent to I-580 and Highway 13. According to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, in 2025, California saw 10,708 crashes involving large trucks, including 232 fatal crashes and 9,753 nonfatal crashes. The increased truck traffic can lead to more accidents on the freeway and endanger pedestrians and cyclists at on- and off-ramps that intersect with city streets. The group believes the CalTrans study will not adequately address the health concerns found in the West Oakland Community Action Plan. They believe that addressing pollution from stationary sources like the port and airport will help the community more than re-routing trucks to I-580. They also support expanding and electrifying rail service and developing dedicated truck lanes on I-880 to reduce congestion and environmental impacts and improve safety by separating trucks from passenger vehicles. To learn more, visit https:// www.nobigrigs580.org/. To sign up for the listening sessions: https://www.nobigrigs580.org/ resources/#Events.

articles.text: Researchers have found that play is not just enjoyable, it is deeply important for learning, creativity, and emotional health. Play has been linked to improved problem-solving, lower stress levels, stronger social bonds, and greater cognitive flexibility. In other words, play helps our brains stay adaptable and open to new ideas. That may be one reason why some of our best ideas seem to arrive when we are relaxed enough to stop forcing them. Somewhere along the way, though, many of us start treating play like it is extra or optional. The thing we will get to after the “important things” are finished. But, the problem is that the important things are literally never finished. There will always be another email, another responsibility, another thing to improve, solve, clean, optimize, or manage. So, play gets pushed farther and farther to the edges until it starts to feel almost irresponsible or, even worse, silly. And yet, play is often where creativity first shows up. Play that just exists for its own sake, not for productivity or strategy, but just for fun and enjoyment. Examples: Doodling silly faces in the margins of a notebook. Singing loudly in the car to your favorite song. Tossing a ball with your kid. Making up a ridiculous backstory for the person walking three dogs at once. What I find interesting is that play changes the way we pay attention. It loosens something inside of us. Play can interrupt the constant pressure to perform or produce. For a moment, we stop trying to get things right and start interacting with the world a little more freely. Children do this naturally, but adults often need to relearn it. So here is a small experiment: find one moment of play this week that has no outcome attached to it. No self-improvement angle. No side hustle potential. No hidden productivity goal. Just one small moment where enjoyment is enough. Maybe it lasts thirty seconds or twenty minutes, the length doesn’t matter. The point is to remember that creativity is not fueled only by discipline and effort. Sometimes it is fueled by lightness and curiosity. Let yourself interact with the world without immediately turning the experience into something useful. Ironically, this is often when new ideas show up anyway. You don’t have to chase new ideas, if you give them room to breathe. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School and High School Music Departments invite the community to their annual Spring Concerts, featuring performances by instrumental and choral music students. All concerts will be held at the Alan Harvey Theater on the Piedmont High School campus. • Tuesday, May 19th at 7:00 p.m. The evening will kick off with the Middle School Orchestra directed by Shauna Revelli. Experience a rich and dynamic program featuring arrangements of timeless masterpieces by J.S. Bach and Ralph Vaughan Williams, alongside the electrifying energy of Coldplay’s Viva la Vida. The evening reaches a finale with the combined 6th–12th grade orchestra musicians performing Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns, under the direction of PHS and PMS music teachers Trevor Chaix and Revelli. • Wednesday, May 20th at 7:00 p.m. The Middle School bands, under the direction of Mary Rees, will light up the stage with the music of Michael Jackson and The Weeknd, a vibrant arrangement of Stevie Wonder’s iconic funk classic Superstition, and the evocative One Summer’s Day from the anime film Spirited Away. In addition, the PHS Jazz Band will make a cameo appearance. • Thursday, May 21st at 7:00 p.m. The final concert of the week features four PHS ensembles – Choir, String Orchestra, Symphonic Band, and Jazz Band – under the direction of Trevor Chaix. The evening concludes with the presentation of the Senior Music Awards. Travel from the big screen to the concert hall with music from Mulan, Ratatouille, How to Train Your Dragon, and La La Land. The Choir will bring the spirit of the ‘60s to life with hits from The Beach Boys, The Mamas and the Papas, and The Beatles. The Symphonic Band will have you grooving to the timeless sounds of ABBA, while the Orchestra performs the beloved Carnival of the Animals by Camille Saint-Saëns. And don’t miss the Jazz Band’s take on Love Me or Leave Me, famously performed by Ella Fitzgerald. Admission To help offset concert expenses a $5 donation is requested. Students attend for free.

articles.text: New PHS records set by Aubrecht, Mumtaz, Iroh Piedmont’s track and field team had a wildly successful day at the 2026 Western Alameda County Conference Championships at Burrell Field in San Leandro on Wednesday and Friday, May 6-8. With topsix finishes, the Highlanders are set to send at least 30 athletes in different events to the North Coast Section Bayshore Area meet at Hayward High on Saturday, May 16. Piedmont athletes broke several school records in the process. Ju n ior spr i nter Clai re Aubrecht finished the 100 meter dash in second of 42 athletes with a time of 12.54. Her time beat Breah Bell’s school record of 12.55 set in 2024. She also improved her school record time in the 200 meters to 25.92 and was second of 36 runners. The time eclipsed her previous best of 26.15 set on March 14 at the San Leandro Invitational. “I was super excited and didn’t believe it at first. It was really cool because I looked up to Breah for a long time. I’ve been through a learning process and need to believe in myself a bit more. I work year-round with a couple of breaks and just put in a ton of time and effort,” Aubrecht said. Teammate Uzoma Iroh also set the school’s shot put record with a distance of 34 feet, 4.5 inches to place fourth of 28. She beat Andrea Martin’s record by three inches set at last year’s WACC Championships. Iroh also set the school record in the discus with a throw of 107 feet, 2 inches, topping Alina Shahid’s 2025 mark by nearly seven inches, while finishing fourth of 27. “Claire and Uzoma are two ladies that have invested the time and energy year round.. We knew they were both going to make noise this year, so taking down these school records isn’t too much of a surprise,” coach Assadi said. On the boys’ side, junior sprinter Rehan Mumtaz broke the school 100 meter record with a time of 11.04 seconds, placing third of 42 runners. He topped Sam Shelby’s 2025 record by .01 of a second. “I was really happy, It’s been a lot of hard work. It feels great to finally have my name on the record board. Hopefully I’ll get to 10.9 soon. Since my freshman year, all I’ve been thinking about is getting my name on that board,” Mumtaz said. Mumtaz mentioned that he’s been dealing with a lingering injury, making his record time all that more special. “I was injured recently and peaked midseason. I started plateauing and stopped working out as hard after getting injured. This week, I decided to forget everything. I had a bone bruise in my heel and an issue with my tendon,” Mumtaz said. Piedmont High’s swimming team competed at the North Coast Section Championships May 7-9 at the College of Marin in Novato. In the process, they qualified two boys’ relay teams to the CIF State Championships at Clovis West HS in Fresno on Thursday and Saturday, May 14-16. Connor Carnazzo was eighth of 16 in the 100 butterfly finals in 50.41, qualifying by placing seventh of 40 in the prelims in 50.06. He also placed 11th of 16 in the 100 backstroke in 51.53, while he qualified for the finals by finishing 12th of 40 in the prelims in 52.11. To get there, he was 10th of 40 in the prelims in 21.27. He was also 11th in the 100 free in 46.52, while he placed ninth in the prelims in 46.39. articles.text: Lucas Smolko (left) stands with the NCS first-place banner alongside Kingston Vora of Lick-Wilmerding, Edward Mofit of Stuart Hall, and Sze Ting Chen of Acalanes. Piedmont High senior Lucas Smolko is putting a bow on his high school career in a big way. On Saturday, May 9, Smolko won the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament’s singles title, beating Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3 at the Marin Tennis Club in San Rafael. To get there, Smolko played as clean a tournament as you could possibly ask, winning every match in straight sets. He won 6-0, 6-0 over St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson in the opening round, followed up with a 6-1, 6-4 win over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and dominated Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. “I was anticipating that match against Sze Ting in the final, so I wanted to make sure I did everything possible to get ready for that match. I just tried to do things in my control; getting properly prepared and trying to finish those early rounds as efficiently as possible,” Smolko said. His win over Chen was a reversal of Piedmont’s February 26 match with Acalanes when Smolko lost 6-3, 7-6. “He played really well both times I played him. The first time I played him, he was serving really great and hitting big, I wasn’t quite ready. This time, I knew what was coming. I knew I had to focus on my own service game and make sure I was holding because his serve is really hard to break,” Smolko said. During the match, Smolko started taking control after Chen won games during Smolko’s Lucas’ serve, shifting his focus to win games as the returner. “There were two turning points. He broke my serve midway through the first set on a deuce point, so I got frustrated and went to reset. I focused up and won the next three games. Seconds set was a similar story. I was up and he broke my serve, but I kept it together and won the last couple of games,” Smolko said. Smolko’s title win marked his third time reaching the finals in his high school career. As a freshman, he fell 6-3, 6-1 to Gus Grumet of University, who later played at Stanford. As a junior, he lost in a three-set battle to Dylan Donovan of Head-Royce. This time, Smolko felt his game elevated to a different point. “It was a fitting ending to my career, for sure. I learned a lot from each tournament, I don’t think I was ready to win it any of the previous years. Freshman year, my level wasn’t high enough. Last year, I wasn’t quite there physically. This year, I was mentally strong and I was able to stay steady physically,” Smolko said. But his Piedmont career isn’t over just yet. He suited up in Purple yesterday, Tuesday, May 11 in the Division 1 NCS Team Tournament with the Highlanders as the No. 12 seed visiting No. 5 San Ramon Valley. “Looking back on it, it’s been a perfect journey. I’ve had to learn and improve a lot throughout my whole career. I’ve really enjoyed it and just being part of a team because tennis is such an individual sport. I’m going to miss it,” Smolko said. articles.text: No. 6 Piedmont fell 7-6 to No. 3 Miramonte in the Division 2 NCS Quarterfinals, ending its season. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team’s season came to an end in the Division 2 North Coast Section Quarterfinals, narrowly falling short of upsetting No. 3 Miramonte. As the No. 6 seed, the Highlanders lost 7-6 on Thursday, May 7. The Highlanders tied the match four different times, but just couldn’t find the go-ahead goal. “It was a hard-fought game on both sides. I thought we played really well on both sides of the ball. We were missing starters on defense but guys stepped up who haven’t really played all season,” coach Andy Kittler said. “It was a close battle, we played with a lot of grit. We had a lot of guys out throughout the season, but I’m super proud of the guys who stepped up,” junior Connor Fredericks mentioned. Despite the loss, the Highlanders’ defense maintained a heavy press for all four quarters, forcing several key turnovers that led to goals. It was something they struggled to do near the end of the regular season. “It came together in the run-up to the game. We had some wakeup calls, so we really put an emphasis on playing as a team and bringing all the energy we could. They put a lot of effort and mental energy into preparing,” Kittler said. To reach the quarterfinals, Piedmont defeated No. 11 Las Lomas 12-11 in overtime on Tuesday, May 5. Piedmont finishes its season with a 7-8 overall record in Kittler’s first year at the helm. It marks a noticeable improvement from last year’s 4-11 finish. “We had an inexperienced team overall and lost some of our experienced guys, so we had to rely on people filling the gaps. We have a lot of athletes who are turning into lacrosse players, we’re convincing them that they can be great players,” Kittler said. “Something we say in the locker room is: ‘Freight Train Energy,’ we kind of lived by that all season. It’s about not stopping and always giving 100 percent,” Fredericks added. But there are some clear building blocks going toward 2027. Key players like Fredericks, Richmond, Owen Curran, Landon Heppner, Deniz Radzik and Milo Stevenson will be seniors. “The majority of our starters are juniors and underclassmen. I’m really looking forward to my senior year, we’re going to have a great team. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High senior Lucas Smolko is putting a bow on his high school career in a big way. On Saturday, May 9, Smolko won the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tournament’s singles title, beating Acalanes’ Sze Ting Chen in straight sets 6-4, 6-3 at the Marin Tennis Club in San Rafael. To get there, Smolko played as clean a tournament as you could possibly ask, winning every match in straight sets. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team suffered a first-round loss to Mt. Eden in the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division tournament, falling 18-5 at the Monarchs’ field in Hayward. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 12-10 as they approach the North Coast Section postseason. Despite the loss, it was a big game for Edie Elmquist, who hit a triple for two RBIs. Talia Perl also logged a triple, while senior Sa’Mara Levi returned to the lineup near the end of the regular season from her travel-ball team to hit a double and two RBIs. The Highlanders approach NCS as the No. 79 ranked team in the section, per Maxpreps.com. According to the NCS’ website, postseason brackets will feature up to 16 teams across six divisions, making it unclear if the top three seeds will receive firstround byes like last season. If the brackets have 16 schools each, PHS would be on track for a Division 5 berth. Their official seeding will be released on Sunday, May 17. Game Recap Mt. Eden led 11-0 following a big bottom of the first inning, and scored four more in the bottom of the second. Both teams scored once in the third inning, while Piedmont scored four times in the top of the fourth. The Monarchs scored twice in the bottom of the fourth and held PHS scoreless in the top of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule. In the third inning, Makenna Small got on base via a catcher’s interference. Edie Elmquist followed up with a bunt single. Kajsa Benson advanced both runners with a bunt of her own, while Staff Photos Freshman Talia Perl had a triple against Mt. Eden, to go along with a run scored. Sa’Mara Levi brought in Small with a groundout to second. Piedmont’s four-run top of the fourth got started with a one-out triple by Talia Perl, smacking it to the right field fence. After that, Samantha Schey hit a hard ground ball back to the pitcher, causing an error to reach first and bring in Perl from third. With two outs, Small drew a walk, and then Elmquist cracked a triple of her own on a line drive to the right field fence— scoring Small and Schey. After Benson drew a walk, Levi hit a double to left field to bring Elmquist home. Final stats: Perl went 2-for-3 with a triple and one run scored. Elmquist went 2-for-4 with a triple, two RBIs and one run scored. Levi went 1-for-2 with a double and two RBIs. Schey had one RBI and one run scored. Small scored two run. articles.text: 9 rowers qualify for Youth Nationals Ten Piedmont rowers brought home medals from the US Rowing Southwest Youth Regional Championships outside Sacramento over the weekend of May 1 to 3. Their wins helped Oakland Strokes record two historic gold medals and qualify 10 boats for the Youth Nationals. The qualifying boats, including nine of the 10 Piedmont athletes, are now headed to the US Rowing Youth National Championships in Sarasota, Florida, in June. Three Piedmont athletes rowed in the Women’s Varsity 8+, which won the gold medal, the club’s first Women’s V8+ title in 12 years: junior Sophia Brenner of Piedmont High in the two seat, senior Claire von Metzsch of College Prep in the five seat, and senior Geneva Johnson of Piedmont High at stroke. The boat is coached by Piedmont resident Allison Ray. The Men’s U17 8+, coached by Sean Gibel, also took gold, the club’s first-ever win in the event’s A Final. Piedmont rowers anchored five more Oakland Strokes boats that qualified for Nationals. Senior Laurel Minor of Piedmont High rowed bow in the Women’s 2V 8+, which took silver. Minor will attend the University of Virginia in the fall. Sophomores Paige Young (bow) and Amelia Callaway (stroke), both of Piedmont High, were in the Women’s 3V 8+ that finished fourth in the 2V A Final to qualify. Sophia Brenner also rowed in the Women’s Pair, which took silver. Claire von Metzsch (bow) and Geneva Johnson (stroke), both V8+ rowers, doubled up in the Women’s Straight Four, which finished fourth and qualified for Nationals. Featured in the boat were Piedmont High senior Geneva Johnson (second from left), Piedmont resident and College Prep senior Claire von Metzsch (fifth from left), and Piedmont junior Sophia Brenner (second from right) Photos by Joel Flory Oakland Strokes Women’s 3V placed fourth to reach Nationals. Piedmont sophomores Paige Young (left) and Amelia Calloway (right) were members if the boat. seat) of Piedmont High were in the Men’s Four which took silver to qualify. Piedmont sophomore Diego Branneria rowed bow in the Men’s Pair (with senior Russell Arroyo of St. Mary’s at stroke), which qualified for Nationals. Senior Audrey Dickinson of Piedmont High also brought home a medal: she rowed in the four seat of an Oakland Strokes 4V crew that took silver in the Women’s Youth 3V 8+ A Final, earning a regional medal. The race is not a Nationals-qualifying event. Dickinson will attend UC Santa Barbara in the fall. The Women’s Varsity 8+ that won gold reflects the strength of the Oakland Strokes pathway to college rowing. All six seniors in the boat are headed to NCAA programs in the fall. Piedmont rowers Geneva Johnson of Piedmont High will attend Boston University, and Claire von Metzsch of College Prep is headed to Yale. Their teammates Ava Wheeler is bound for the University of Pennsylvania, Alexis Arroyo for Tufts, the coxswain Samyra Joshi for Duke, and Mako Begossi for the University of California, Berkeley. Senan Brodie of Piedmont High has committed to row for Penn lightweights in the fall. In total 15 Oakland Strokes seniors will row at college programs across the country in the fall. “What I’m most proud of is that the entire team worked for these results,” said Allison Ray, the Oakland Strokes Director of Rowing. “Sending the 1V, 2V, and 3V to Nationals together is a first for our club, and it happened because everyone felt part of the work, whether they were in those top boats or not. That speaks to the strength of Oakland.” “What I’m most proud of is the culture this squad built, working hard, being coachable, and lifting up their teammates,” said Sean Gibel, the Oakland Strokes Men’s U17/U16 Coach. “The goal was to put in the work to be a front-runner, not just a contender. Now we enter Nationals training as front-runners from the Southwest. And one of the best parts of the weekend was watching families and teammates cheering for every Oakland boat down the course. Different squads, one team.” Oakland Strokes is for athletes who want to be inspired, challenged, and compete at the highest level. The club has programs for middle schoolers and high schoolers, with no rowing experience required. Summer camps for middle and high school athletes and middle school yearround programs are open for registration now. The high school team also offers a free two-week trial in late August for athletes considering joining. For 50 years on the Oakland Estuary, Oakland Strokes has sent rowers to the most competitive programs in the country, where rowing has opened doors at schools many of them might not otherwise have reached. Information about all programs and registration is available at www.oaklandstrokes.org. Next Up Oakland Strokes qualified 10 boats for Youth Nationals. articles.text: The road warrior PMS Scots softball team continued with another slate of 4 away games last week, posting a perfect 4-0 record, making this a stellar 7-1 road trip. The Scots opened the week on Monday, May 4, with a dominant 17-2 win vs Berkeley’s King Middle School Cobras. All facets were on display with Bailey Gregovich and Sarina Hill combining to defang the Cobras by allowing just 2 hits over four innings and notching 9 strikeouts while getting flawless support from the defense. The offensive effort was led by Alice Sorensen’s 4 RBIs, including legging out a homerun in the 3rd inning that set off a frenzy in the Piedmont dugout. Bailey Gregovich followed up by unleashing a bomb to right field in the 4th that looked destined to be the second HR of the afternoon but was limited to a standup triple thanks to an ill-considered stop sign by third base coach Alex Joerger. Mackenzie Ewen (3-3, 3 RBI) and Nina Stock (2 RBI) also had key contributions at the plate. On Tuesday, May 5, the Scots were back in action vs Berkeley’s Longfellow Middle School that saw the Scots come away with a 14-5 victory. Though the offense was generated largely from free passes and aggressive base running, there was some extra power on display from Simone Tornatore (2-2, 4 RBI) and Evie Joerger (2B, RBI, 3 runs scored). In Oakland, on Wednesday, May 6, the Scots faced a new opponent, the West Oakland Phoenix , who fielded a team of largely novice players that noneCatcher Simone Tornatore celebrates after her dramatic tag-out to end the May 8 game against Montera. Piedmont Middle school’s softball team recently went 4-0 on its road stand. Pictured are front row) Nina Stock (left), Olive Dao-Hoang, Simone Tornatore, Madi Farboud, Keira Spina, (back row) Coach Luke Blanchard (left), Alice Sorenson, Sarina Hill, Mackenzie Ewen, Abby Gregovich, Anya Giri, Coach Steve Gregovich, Cate Penrod, Clara Blanchard, and Bailey Gregovich. theless kept the game very tight as the Scots clung to a 1-0 lead through three innings. Piedmont ultimately broke through and prevailed 9-0 thanks to a pair of doubles from Mackenzie Ewen’s hot bat (2-2, 3 RBI) and Clara Blanchard’s pair of RBIs that complemented her three strong defensive plays that helped keep the Phoenix from ever spreading their wings. Friday’s fourth and final game saw the much-anticipated rematch vs the undefeated Montera Toros, who had handed the Scots a gut-wrenching loss in walk-off fashion barely a week prior. Fans were not disappointed as the teams combined for another electric show on the diamond and this time Piedmont seized the moment, ending the game with a dramatic tag-out by catcher Simone Tornatore on an attempted steal of home that sealed the 8-7 triumph. The 8th grade pitching aces, Madi Farboud and Bailey Gregovich, again carried the load from the circle, allowing only 6 hits and notching 11 strikeouts over 6 innings of work. articles.text: Photo by Genesis Botello “Postcards from Dvořák” will run July 11 through 26 at venues throughout Sonoma county. The Valley of the Moon Music Festival returns for its 12th season this summer with a program celebrating the music and global influences of Czech composer Antonín Dvořák. Titled “Postcards from Dvořák,” the festival will run July 11 through 26 at venues throughout Sonoma County, combining chamber music performances on historical instruments with outdoor concerts, lectures and family programming. Led by festival co-founders and directors Tanya Tomkins and Eric Zivian, the 2026 season explores the people, places and cultural traditions that shaped Dvořák’s music during his travels across Europe and the United States. “Dvořák is a natural choice to anchor our 12th season,” Zivian said in a statement. “While deeply rooted in musical tradition, he was remarkably open to cultural influences from around the world — traveling extensively and embracing new ideas in ways that were rare for a 19th-century composer.” “His openness, heartfelt musical voice, and deep respect for other traditions continue to inspire us,” Tomkins added. “For us, he represents the power of music to bring people together across cultures and communities.” The season features seven mainstage programs at Hanna Center Auditorium, beginning July 11 with “Bohemian Homeland,” an opening-night concert inspired by Dvořák’s roots in 19th-century Prague. The festival concludes July 26 with “Final Years: Going Home,” a finale celebrating Dvořák’s return to Bohemia. Other programs include “English Impressions,” exploring connections between English and Bohemian musical traditions, and “American Roots,” highlighting the composer’s years in the United States and the influence of African American spirituals and American folk music on his work. The festival also will present music by composers including Johannes Brahms, Felix Mendelssohn, Florence Price, Harry T. Burleigh and Leoš Janáček. Organizers said the programming reflects the festival’s ongoing effort to broaden the classical canon and highlight underrepresented composers. Guest artists this season include violinists Rachell Ellen Wong, Jennifer Frautschi, Elizabeth Blumenstock and Tien-Hsin Cindy Wu. The Amizia Quartet will return as the festival’s Fellowship Quartet-in-Residence. In addition to ticketed performances, the festival will offer pay-what-you-wish outdoor concerts, a free family concert at the Sonoma Community Center and pre-concert lectures curated by Kate van Orden. Tickets and passes are available online at valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org. articles.text: The 32nd annual Sculpture in the Garden at Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek will be on view June 13 through August 9, featuring more than 80 sculptures from 42 artists. The event is the nonprofit’s longest-running annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural pieces with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. A range of returning local artists, as well as newcomers, are participating this year. Sculpture in the Garden also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake, was a pioneer in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Garden is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraisers like Sculpture in the Garden. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/2025-sculpture-in-thegarden/. More than 80 sculptures will be available for purchase this year. articles.text: The opera marks the return of Spanish director Emilio Sagi’s staging, first introduced in 2013. The San Francisco Opera opens its 2026 summer season on May 28 with Gioachino Rossini’s comic opera The Barber of Seville. The opera, featuring two international casts and conducted by Benjamin Manis, also marks the return of Spanish director Emilio Sagi’s staging, first introduced by the company in 2013 and revived in 2015. The production is a co-production with the Lithuanian National Opera and Ballet Theatre. Rossini composed The Barber of Seville in 1816 in just 13 days to meet a deadline from an impresario. Though its Rome premiere was widely considered a failure, the opera later became one of the most frequently performed works in the repertory. The opera follows Figaro, a resourceful barber, as he helps Count Almaviva win the affection of Rosina while outmaneuvering her guardian, Doctor Bartolo. The score includes well-known arias such as “Largo al factotum” and “Una voce poco fa.” American baritones Joshua Hopkins and Justin Austin will alternate in the title role. Mezzo-sopranos Maria Kataeva and Hongni Wu share the role of Rosina. Tenors Levy Sekgapane and Jack Swanson will make company debuts as Count Almaviva. Additional cast members include Renato Girolami, Patrick Carfizzi and Catherine Cook, who reprises the role of Berta after performing it in every San Francisco Opera presentation of The Barber of Seville since 1996. The third performance of The Barber of Seville on Friday, June 5 will be livestreamed. Tickets, which includes a 48-hour on-demand viewing window that begins June 7 at 10 a.m., may be purchased online at sfopera.com/ digital/livestream. All live performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House on May 28 (7:30 p.m.); June 3 (7:30 p.m.), 5 (7:30 p.m.), 6 (2 p.m.), 9 (7:30 p.m.), 12 (7:30 p.m.), 13 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (2 p.m.), 21 (2 p.m.). Visit sfopera.com to purchase tickets.

Cantabella fosters choral artistry through the performance of music from all genres. They enhance music literacy using the Kodaly method as their pedagogical method. articles.text: Star Wars returns to theaters with a trusty duo, in theaters May 22 After seven years away from the big screen, Star Wars returns with its most reliable characters. The Mandalorian and Grogu brings Din Djarin and his Force-sensitive ward from Disney Plus to IMAX, trading streaming convenience for theatrical spectacle. The gamble appears to be paying off. Director Jon Favreau, who turned a bounty hunter and his adopted alien child into Disney Plus’s biggest phenomenon, now faces a different challenge: proving these characters deserve cinema real estate. Early screenings suggest he has cleared that hurdle, delivering action sequences designed for the biggest screens while maintaining the tone that made the series work. The plot picks up after the show’s third season. The New Republic enlists Djarin and Grogu to rescue Rotta the Hutt, son of the late Jabba, in exchange The Mandalorian and Grogu premiers in theaters May 22 for intelligence on Imperial remnants still threatening the galaxy. The mission structure gives Favreau room for what he does best: kinetic action, creature cantinas and that peculiar father-son dynamic between armored warrior and tiny green toddler. Production filmed entirely in California, a first for a Star Wars theatrical release, using a combination of practical sets and the Volume technology that revolutionized the series. The production received one of the largest allocations in California’s filming tax incentive program history, which speaks to the scale Lucasfilm wanted.

In my experience, the most difficult part of painting buildings is not finding the painting contractor, not the scraping, sanding or surface preparation, not dealing with the mess. The most difficult part is the selection of colors. Maybe this is because like most aspects of the architectural field, color selection is a curious mix of art and science, and…we all experience colors differently. Balancing the main color attributes of hue (color: red, blue, etc.), intensity (saturation or purity), and value (lightness/ darkness i.e., tints/shades) with other associated variables is simply a difficult job. In the end, from the bold, emotion-evoking colors of Mexican architects such as the famous Luis Barragan, to the restrained, subtle colors we are most familiar with in the Bay Area, exterior colors on a building reveal, perhaps more than anything else, the attitudes, ideas and personality of the owners. Building colors should first respond to the character, style, and detailing of the architecture. Schemes with multiple colors require a natural stopping/starting point for color changes such as a different material or corners and offsets in wall planes. Certain interior colors need also be coordinated, most notably curtains and shades which are seen through the windows and have to work with the exterior colors. Because all urban buildings are surrounded by neighboring buildings, as well as landscape planting, paving, and other elements, exterior color selection necessarily also involves urban design considerations; each building is part of a larger neighborhood palate. Evaluation of color requires certain steps to be successful. Most importantly, although not nearly done often enough, is to allow enough time for color selection and approval before painting starts. Once an attipainted on at least two different walls of the building with different natural light conditions. These must be allowed to dry for at least a few days before being evaluated. It is good for owners to then reflect on the samples at different times of the day for a good week before modifications are made or final approval given. This is all pretty complex, at least to me. If it’s one thing I’ve learned is that professional help (and patience) is essential in color selection. Color is mysterious, and what it does to the psyche is diverse. But the measure of success is simple in the end. It is the answer to the question: do you like it? Does it make you glad to be at that place? Does it, as Marie Kondo would ask, bring you joy? The weather was overcast and cool, so the group set up chairs inside the hall. They were there to talk about their May book, The God of the Woods by Liz Moore, a mystery novel. It was named a New York Times “Notable Book of the Year” and People Magazine’s #1 Book of the Year for 2024. This is the story of the disappearance of the daughter of the wealthy Van Laar family from their summer camp in 1975. It is very similar to the unsolved disappearance of her older brother years before. The setting is the camp, the Adirondack Mountains, and the Van Laar’s lavish estate. Within the plot, there are long-buried secrets of the affluent Van Laar family and the working-class community that serves them. As an inexperienced investigator unravels the mystery, a multi-threaded sequence of events with themes of class tension, family secrets, and the search for truth. The previous month, the group had read Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets by Belarusian Svetlana Alexievich, for which she won the Nobel Prize. This book tells the story of the demise of the USSR’s communist state through the feelings of everyday people as the country transitioned to capitalism. It may be an important book, but it is also a hard book to get through. It seemed the readers were ready for something lighter this month, and they had it with The God of the Woods. At just under 500 pages, it is not short but could be breezed through. It was a good not-quite-summer read. In fact, one reader listened to the audio version on a drive around Hawaii. The book brought back some readers’ childhood, summer camp memories, and experiences in the Adirondacks. The book was “a cut above most mysteries.” Many readers thought the novel was “fine,” but had issues with it. Generally, they “liked it,” but didn’t “love it” or “hate it.” It was an easy read, but “not great literature.” The readers enjoyed the relationships of the more than 40 characters, but some members of the group had to make lists to keep track of them. Readers found the dates at the start of each chapter helpful for keeping track of the narrative, but others didn’t like the author’s use of the common writer technique of short chapters and bouncing back and forth in time. Readers had issues with the characters, too. They didn’t like any of them. They were either all good or all bad people, and the rich were all bad people. That didn’t seem real. The townpeople On hand were Marj Blackwell, Nancy Henn, Mary Carter, Lois Price, Gerry Gragg, Bill Ahern, Rob White, Adrienne Hamlin, Tim Weishahn, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Ken Young, Dale Benveniste, Lisa Euphrat, Susan Southworth, Rich Seigel, Odette Pollar, Susie Backer, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The God of the Woods written by Liz Moore were the rock on which the rich people depended. The book’s ending seemed “unbelievable,” “lame,” and even “hilarious” for one reader. Another reader found it surprising that the book was on the New York Times’ notable books list for the year. Overall, The God of the Woods was generally liked, but not loved. It was an entertaining mystery and an easy read. The stark difference from last month’s novel started a discussion about which of the two was a better or more worthwhile use of the readers’ time. This sparked reactions. “Could a book be a better read if 80% of the group didn’t want to read it?” “Aren’t there different reasons to read different types of books?” “Could a book be a medicine that might not taste good, but would make us better?” All good questions to be considered. However, the group seemed to agree that The God of the Woods was enjoyable and that was what the doctor had ordered for their May book. The readers had previously selected Barbarian Days – A Surfing Life by William Finnegan for its June book and Old Filth by English author Jane Gardam for July. Darby Gragg could not be with them this month, so Lois Price presented her three non-fiction candidates for the group’s August read, and the readers selected The Art Thief by Michael Finkel. With all their business done, they took a group photo on the patio outside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on June 1 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. articles.text: The Wednesday before Mother’s Day meant it was time for the Piedmont Recreation Department Walking on Wednesdays group’s annual visit to the Morcom Rose Garden, up Jean Street on the other side of Grand Avenue. A good turnout of 38 walkers and six K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra on a lovely morning. As the walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue, they passed Nanci’s Musiktime near the Exedra, where young children were making music on the grass above the park’s tot lot. Also sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the program serves children ages 0 to 5 with singing, dancing, puppetry and instrument play led by instructor Nanci Schneidinger. The classes meet at the same time and place as Walking on Wednesdays. Continuing down Magnolia to Wildwood Avenue, the walkers passed homes lined with roses, California golden and yellow poppies, Mexican sage, birds-of-paradise and even a few dandelions in bloom. Near Grand Avenue, they encountered another Wednesday walking group. Children ages five and younger from Wildwood Children’s School were headed to the Dearing Park Wildwood Triangle for playtime beneath the redwoods. The children were all connected by a rope, prompting one walker to suggest something similar might better keep the Wednesday walkers together, too. The group paused briefly at Grand Avenue for an update on the long-delayed Shell Recharging Station project before crossing over and heading up Jean Street to the Morcom Rose Garden. At the entrance, framed by Sally Holmes roses in full bloom, the group gathered for a photo and a quick history lesson. articles.text: In 1910, a group of Piedmont Church’s founding members gathered together to compose a Creed. The words reflect both the inclusive vision and the enduring mission that have guided our church for over 100 years. We favor a sane, simple and earnest piety, free alike from cant and extravagance. We assume no right to dictate to another his creed, but with charity for one another’s individual peculiarities of belief, we unite on the broad basis of the Christian religion as expressed in the following statements: God – We believe in God as the great Father of us all, who reveals Himself supremely in the person of His Son Christ Jesus our Lord, to whose life and character the Scriptures bear witness; and whose Holy Spirit continually upholds and guides all His children. Ourselves – We believe in trying to realize within ourselves lives of goodness, beauty, strength, and peace; and that the noblest career is one of mutual trust and helpfulness, after the example of Him who “went about doing good.” Others – But, besides believing that the principles of Christianity tend to the highest perfection of personal character, we hold that they make possible the greatest peace and happiness of communities, and that their hearty adoption would solve all the domestic and social problems of cities, states or nations. Kalamas had one assist and ground ball. 12-11 win over Las Lomas Piedmont got out to a 6-2 lead in the first quarter and led 8-4 at halftime. Las Lomas limited Owen Curran scored twice against Miramonte. PHS to just one goal in the third and scored four to cut the Highlanders’ lead to 9-8. Las Lomas tied the match at 11-11 with 28 seconds left in the game to force overtime. For the game-winning Golden Goal in overtime, Fredericks won the opening faceoff leading to the goal. Heppner was in possession, attracting a double team as he approached the circle. Heppner quickly worked the ball back to Fredericks, who passed the ball to Richmond making a run from behind the net to just feet in front of the net unmarked. In close distance, Richmond put the shot by the goalie for the winner. Final stats: Fredericks scored five goals, two assists, 10 ground balls, and won 16 face-offs. Kalamas had four goals and one assist. Richmond scored three goals. Ryan Graham scored once. Religion Corner Continued from page 2 learn to forsake their warring madness. As followers of Jesus the question we must face is “Are we teachable.” Are the congregations and communities that profess to follow Jesus teachable? Can we recognize that much of what we do in the name of Jesus is, in fact, far from Christ like? Will we change, adapt, learn? As human beings the question we must face is “Are we teachable?” Can we recognize the destruction that awaits if we continue of worship at the altar of war? Will we change, adapt, learn? Holy One, you created us to be teachable, help us to claim that identity in word and in deed. Amen. Rev. Jim Hopkins is the retired Senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland. The Piedmont Church Creed In 1910, a group of Piedmont Church’s founding members gathered together to compose a Creed. The words reflect both the inclusive vision and the enduring mission that have guided our church for over 100 years. We favor a sane, simple and earnest piety, free alike from cant and extravagance. We assume no right to dictate to another his creed, but with charity for one another’s individual peculiarities of belief, we unite on the broad basis of the Christian religion as expressed in the following statements: God – We believe in God as the great Father of us all, who reveals Himself supremely in the person of His Son Christ Jesus our Lord, to whose life and character the Scriptures bear witness; and whose Holy Spirit continually upholds and guides all His children. Ourselves – We believe in trying to realize within ourselves lives of goodness, beauty, strength, and peace; and that the noblest career is one of mutual trust and helpfulness, after the example of Him who “went about doing good.” Others – But, besides believing that the principles of Christianity tend to the highest perfection of personal character, we hold that they make possible the greatest peace and happiness of communities, and that their hearty adoption would solve all the domestic and social problems of cities, states or nations. WORSHIP IN PERSON OR ONLINE SUNDAYS, 10AM The Past – We revere the past, but cannot fight again its battles. Our religion is not a thing of history, but a reality to be experienced now in fellowship with God and with one another. The Future – We believe in a heaven hereafter and seek to anticipate it here and now by obedience to its laws and the appropriation of its spirit. The Sacraments – We receive the sacraments of Baptism and Communion and hold that baptism should be administered in such mode as the applicant prefers, and that the privileges of the Lord’s Supper should be open to all who call themselves by His name. We cordially invite all who sympathize with our aim, of whatever sect or of none and who are willing to cooperate with us in the spirit of Jesus for the help of one another and for the salvation of mankind, to join with us in our work and worship.
